narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades had the strongest influence. Being in the bottom decile of your class placed you far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the 6th decile. This low ranking strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your third-year grades were the next most important factor; ranking in the second decile again fell well below the accepted-student average near the sixth decile, further increasing the chance of failure.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.40 it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your early class rankings.

Your family income, LSAT score of 32, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in the decision; the model ignored those characteristics.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record in ways that demonstrate consistent high performance, such as excelling in challenging courses or gaining strong recommendation letters that highlight your growth. Consider retaking the LSAT if possible, and apply to a broader range of schools while seeking mentorship or bar-prep resources early. (218 words)
